cells.tense: The practice is running now without force, and it connects you rather than closes you off.
cells.ask: Keep the same practice for one week — same time, same length — and notice on the last day whether it opened something to give away.
cells.core:
You already have a way of working that holds. Same time, same shape, day after day, and the doing of it does not drain you the way it drains people who are forcing it. That steadiness is the whole point; the skill comes as a by-product.

The quiet hours are not a wall around you. You come back from them and you are closer to people, not further. What you make keeps getting a little truer to what you actually are. That is the balance to protect. When the practice turns into a deadline or a score, stop and get back to the plain version. Next, if anything, feed this: when it is steady, speak from it, and watch something false you have been propping up fall away on its own.
cells.sheetLine: Steady practice that opens you rather than closes you off.
cells.verb: keeping the small steady fire lit by showing up again and again
cells.place: the place where what you already are comes to the surface

cells.tense: You are refining for a day that has not arrived, and you cannot put the work down without fear.
cells.ask: Finish something today at the point where it is good enough, and let it sit seen by you or one other person without touching it again.
cells.core:
You keep pushing toward a version that is still a little sharper, a little more finished, and the version keeps moving. So the work does not close, and rest starts to feel like a risk. The hours alone feel necessary now, not chosen. An interruption reads as a threat instead of a break.

What you are protecting is not the work; it is a picture of yourself at the end of a road you cannot see yet. The practice you built to grow is eating the growth. Set something down where it is good enough and leave it. Letting go can be a form of finishing, not a defeat. Trust that what you have made can hold without another pass, and let one thing stand as it is.

cells.tense: You stopped at a door a while back, and something keeps you standing where you are.
cells.ask: Pick one practice and give it ten unhurried minutes today, then put down the clock and go do something else.
cells.core:
You know what it would take — the same small thing, done often. And you do not do it. Not because you cannot, but because it has come to feel like a place you are not supposed to spend time. So you live mostly in the present with the practice just behind you, waiting.

The ability is still there; you have not lost it. What is missing is the easy give and take of your own effort. Start with a little, a very little, and let it count. Ten unhurried minutes is enough to begin. Then let it go for the day. Keep showing up without pressure and the practice starts to feel like air again, not a door.
cells.sheetLine: The ability is still there. What stopped was the showing up.

cells.tense: You are practising right now, and you would describe it as something that just happens.
cells.ask: Name one thing you can do well and trace it back to one specific time you tried it and it went badly — say the story out loud once.
cells.core:
People call you a natural. You do not experience the work that made it that way — the repetitions, the trying and failing, the small corrections. It arrives as a gift you cannot quite account for. Or it is a thing you keep refusing to call practice, because calling it that would mean it counts.

The skill is real and it is yours, but you have not claimed it. You have been carrying it as luck or as something that slipped in without your participation. Look at how you got here. There is a body of work behind your competence and you built it. Say that out loud, even just once. Own the method and the imagination has somewhere solid to stand.
cells.sheetLine: You call it natural. It was built, and you built it.
